mn107:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the palace of Migāra’s Mother.
mn107:1.3: Then the accountant Moggallāna the brahmin went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
mn107:1.4: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, the accountant Moggallāna the brahmin said to the Blessed One:
mn107:2.1: ‘Master Gotama, in this palace of Migāra’s Mother there can be seen progressive training, progressive work and progressive practice, that is to say,
mn107:2.2: down to the last step of the stair.[^1]
mn107:2.3: And also in the case of these brahmins there can be seen progressive training, progressive work and progressive practice, that is to say,
mn107:2.5: And also in the case of these archers there can be seen progressive training, progressive work and progressive practice, that is to say,
mn107:2.7: And also in the case of us accountants, who get our living by accountancy, there can be seen progressive training, progressive work and progressive practice, that is to say,
mn107:2.9: For, Master Gotama, when we get an apprentice, we first make him count thus:
mn107:2.10: ‘One, ones; two, twos; three, threes; four, fours; five, fives; six, sixes; seven, sevens; eight, eights; nine, nines; ten, tens.’
mn107:2.11: And we make him count a hundred too, and more than that too.
mn107:2.12: Now, Master Gotama, is it possible, in the case of this Dhamma and Discipline, to describe progressive training, progressive work and progressive practice in the same way?’
mn107:3.1: ‘It is possible, brahmin, in the case of this Dhamma and Discipline to describe progressive training, progressive work and progressive practice.
mn107:3.2: Just as, brahmin, a skilled tamer of horses, on getting a fine thoroughbred, first makes him do exercises with the bit in his mouth, and afterwards makes him do further exercises;
mn107:3.3: so too, brahmin, when the Tathāgata gets a person to be tamed, he first disciplines him thus:
mn107:3.4: ‘Come, bhikkhu, be virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha,[^2] perfect in conduct and resort, and, seeing danger in the slightest fault, train by undertaking the training precepts.’
mn107:4.1: When, brahmin, the bhikkhu is virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and, seeing danger in the slightest fault, trains by undertaking the training precepts, the Tathāgata disciplines him further:
mn107:4.2: ‘Come, bhikkhu, guard the doors of the faculties. On seeing a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs and features.
mn107:4.3: Since, if you left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade you, practise the way of its restraint, guard the eye faculty, undertake the restraint of the eye faculty.
mn107:4.4: On hearing a sound with the ear …
mn107:4.5: on smelling an odour with the nose …
mn107:4.6: on tasting a flavour with the tongue …
mn107:4.7: on touching a tangible with the body …
mn107:4.8: on cognizing a dhamma with the mind, do not grasp at its signs and features.
mn107:4.9: Since, if you left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade you, practise the way of its restraint, guard the mind faculty, undertake the restraint of the mind faculty.’
mn107:5.1: When, brahmin, the bhikkhu guards the doors of the faculties, the Tathāgata disciplines him further:
mn107:5.2: ‘Come, bhikkhu, be one who knows the right amount in eating.
mn107:5.3: Reflecting wisely, you should take food
mn107:5.4: neither for amusement nor for intoxication nor for smartening nor for embellishment, but only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the life divine, thinking: “Thus I shall terminate old feelings without arousing new feelings, and I shall be healthy and blameless and live in comfort.”’[^3]
mn107:6.1: When, brahmin, the bhikkhu knows the right amount in eating, the Tathāgata disciplines him further:
mn107:6.2: ‘Come, bhikkhu, abide devoted to wakefulness. By day, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive dhammas. In the first watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive dhammas. In the middle watch of the night, lie down on the right side in the lion’s pose, with one foot overlapping[^4] the other, mindful and fully aware, having noted in your mind the time for rising. After rising, in the third watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive dhammas.’
mn107:7.1: When, brahmin, the bhikkhu is devoted to wakefulness, the Tathāgata disciplines him further:
mn107:7.2: ‘Come, bhikkhu, possess mindfulness and full awareness. Act in full awareness when going forward and returning; act in full awareness when looking ahead and looking away; act in full awareness when flexing and extending your limbs; act in full awareness when wearing your outer cloak, bowl and robes; act in full awareness when eating, drinking, chewing and tasting; act in full awareness when defecating and urinating; act in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking and keeping silent.’
mn107:8.1: When, brahmin, the bhikkhu possesses mindfulness and full awareness, the Tathāgata disciplines him further:
mn107:8.2: ‘Come, bhikkhu, resort to a secluded resting place—the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, a heap of straw.’
mn107:9.1: He resorts to a secluded resting place—the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, a heap of straw.
mn107:9.2: On returning from his alms round, after his meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
mn107:9.3: Abandoning covetousness for the world, he abides with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
mn107:9.4: Abandoning ill-will and hatred, he abides with a mind free from ill-will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill-will and hatred.
mn107:9.5: Abandoning lethargy and drowsiness, he abides free from lethargy and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and fully aware; he purifies his mind of lethargy and drowsiness.
mn107:9.6: Abandoning agitation and worry, he abides unagitated with a mind stilled within; he purifies his mind of agitation and worry.
mn107:9.7: Abandoning uncertainty, he abides having crossed beyond uncertainty, unperplexed about profitable dhammas; he purifies his mind of uncertainty.
mn107:10.1: Having abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of mind that weaken understanding,
mn107:10.2: quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.
mn107:10.3: With the stilling of initial and sustained application, he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without initial application and without sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of concentration.
mn107:10.4: With the fading as well of happiness, he abides in equanimity, and mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna, on account of which the Noble Ones announce: ‘He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.’
mn107:10.5: With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
mn107:11.1: This, brahmin, is the kind of instruction I give to those bhikkhus who are in higher training, whose minds have not yet attained the goal, who abide aspiring to the supreme surcease of bondage.
mn107:11.2: But for those bhikkhus who are Arahants with taints exhausted, who have lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached the highest goal, destroyed the fetters of being, who, through knowing rightly, are liberated, these dhammas conduce to a pleasant abiding here and now and to mindfulness and full awareness.’
mn107:12.1: When this was said, the accountant Moggallāna the brahmin said to the Blessed One:
mn107:12.2: ‘Master Gotama, when Master Gotama’s disciples are thus advised and instructed by him, do they all attain the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, or do some not attain it?’
mn107:12.3: ‘Brahmin, some of my disciples, when thus advised and instructed by me, attain the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, and some do not attain it.’
mn107:13.1: ‘Master Gotama, since there is Nibbāna, and there is the path leading to Nibbāna, and there is Master Gotama as guide,
mn107:13.2: what is the cause, what is the reason, why, when Master Gotama’s disciples are thus advised and instructed by him, some attain the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, and some do not attain it?’
mn107:14.1: ‘Well then, brahmin, I shall question you about this in return. Answer as you see fit.
mn107:14.3: Are you skilled in the road leading to Rājagaha?’
mn107:14.4: ‘Yes, sir, I am skilled in the road leading to Rājagaha.’
mn107:14.6: Suppose a man came here wanting to go to Rājagaha.
mn107:14.8: “Venerable sir, I want to go to Rājagaha;
mn107:14.9: show me the road to Rājagaha.”
mn107:14.11: “Well, good man, this road goes to Rājagaha.
mn107:14.12: Follow it for a while, and you will see a certain village; follow it for a while, and you will see a certain town;
mn107:14.13: follow it for a while, and you will see Rājagaha with its delightful parks, delightful woods, delightful lands and delightful lotus pools.”
mn107:14.14: Though advised and instructed by you thus, he might take the wrong road and go west.
mn107:14.15: Then a second man came here wanting to go to Rājagaha.
mn107:14.17: “Venerable sir, I want to go to Rājagaha;
mn107:14.18: show me the road to Rājagaha.”
mn107:14.20: “Well, good man, this road goes to Rājagaha.
mn107:14.21: Follow it for a while, and you will see a certain village;
mn107:14.22: follow it for a while, and you will see a certain town;
mn107:14.23: follow it for a while, and you will see Rājagaha with its delightful parks, delightful woods, delightful lands and delightful lotus pools.”
mn107:14.24: Advised and instructed by you thus, he might get safely to Rājagaha.
mn107:14.25: What is the cause, what is the reason, brahmin, why, since there is Rājagaha, and there is the road leading to Rājagaha, and there is you as guide,
mn107:14.26: yet when advised and instructed by you thus, one man takes the wrong road and goes west, and the other gets safely to Rājagaha?’
mn107:14.27: ‘What can I do about that, Master Gotama?
mn107:14.28: I am only one who points out the way, Master Gotama.’
mn107:14.29: ‘So too, brahmin, there is Nibbāna, and there is the path leading to Nibbāna, and there am I as guide;
mn107:14.30: yet when my disciples are thus advised and instructed by me, some attain the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, and some do not attain it.
mn107:14.31: What can I do about that, brahmin?
mn107:14.32: The Tathāgata is only one who points out the way, brahmin.’
mn107:15.1: When this was said, the accountant Moggallāna the brahmin said to the Blessed One:
mn107:15.2: “As to those persons, Master Gotama, who are faithless, who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness not out of faith but seeking a livelihood, who are fraudulent, deceitful, treacherous, haughty,[^5] hollow, vain, rough-tongued, loose-spoken, unguarded in the faculties, immoderate in eating, undevoted to wakefulness, unconcerned with the ascetic life, without deep respect for the training, luxurious, lax, foremost in backsliding, neglectful of seclusion, lazy, lacking energy, unmindful, lacking full awareness, unconcentrated, with wandering minds, witless, and drivelling—Master Gotama does not dwell together with these.
mn107:15.3: But as to those clansmen who have gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, who are not fraudulent, not deceitful, not treacherous, not haughty, not hollow, not vain, not rough-tongued, not loose-spoken, guarded in the faculties, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, concerned with the ascetic life, with deep respect for the training, not luxurious, not lax, foremost in avoiding backsliding, foremost in seclusion, energetic, resolute, with mindfulness set up, fully aware, concentrated, with unified minds, possessing understanding, and not drivelling—Master Gotama dwells together with these.
mn107:16.1: Just as, of root perfumes of any kind, black orris root is reckoned the best;
mn107:16.2: of heartwood perfumes of any kind, red sandalwood is reckoned the best;
mn107:16.3: of flower perfumes of any kind, jasmine is reckoned the best;
mn107:16.4: so too, Master Gotama’s advice is supreme among the dhammas of the present day.
mn107:17.2: Master Gotama has made the Dhamma clear in many ways, as though he were turning upright what had been overthrown, revealing what was hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the dark for those with eyes to see forms.
mn107:17.3: I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
mn107:17.4: From today let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone to him for refuge for life.’”
